title: Stanovanje
reviewerNotes: This full draft is ready for human review before publication.
storyBeat: Ana and Emir visit a Zenica flat with Amira and almost sign a monthly lease with the landlord.

vocabulary: Name stan, soba, kirija, and namještaj for a rental visit.
Use može and moraš as present permission and obligation chunks.
Ask Koliko je kirija? and talk about a monthly stay.
grammar: Use Može? and Može. as quick permission lines.
Say moraš with rent and contract nouns in the present.
Describe a flat with ima and soba phrases.
culture: Picture apartment hunting in Zenica near schools and tram lines.
Treat a hallway tour as polite present-tense practice.
Notice how returnees and young families compete for the same flats.

grammar.title: Može permission chunks
grammar.explanation: Learn this as a full phrase. Do not treat it as a table. Može? asks if something is allowed. Može. answers yes in one calm word. Ne može. refuses without a tense chart. Pair the chunk with ulazite or sjedite when you visit a flat.

examples.english: May I? Can I look at the apartment?
Not allowed. There is no key.

grammar.title: Moraš obligation lines
grammar.explanation: Hold this as a spoken pattern. Do not treat it as a grammar grid. Moraš tells one person what they must do now. Add platiti kiriju or imati ugovor right after the chunk. Stay in the present so the landlord talk stays practical.

grammar.title: Rent question shape
grammar.explanation: Take this as a speaking chunk. Do not memorize a case chart yet. Ask Koliko je kirija? when you stand in the hallway. Answer Kirija je mjesečno. Add a number later. The question shape matters more than every case ending today.

culture.title: Flat hunting in Zenica
culture.body: In Zenica many newcomers hunt flats through word of mouth, online ads, and quick visits after work. Ana and Emir climb a staircase in a block near the steelworks and imagine a longer stay beyond the guest room above the café. The landlord opens a bright kitchen and points to a corner where a sofa already waits. Kirija is discussed in marks per month on a handwritten note taped to the door. Young families and returnees often compete for the same two-room flats near schools and tram lines. A polite visit with molim and clear questions about rent can turn a hallway tour into a serious conversation about keys.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A. Permission and rent questions
lessonBlocks.body: Start with stan, soba, and kirija so the hallway has real nouns before you step inside. Practice Može? Mogu pogledati stan? until the permission chunk sounds natural at a closed door. Ask Koliko je kirija? while you still wear your shoes in the corridor. Add kuhinja and kupatilo as you walk through each room. Ana repeats mjesečno with the landlord while Emir counts windows and checks the light. Keep može and moraš as spoken lines rather than a modal verb table. Point at namještaj in the corner and say ima mali sto. Reuse molim when you enter and hvala when you leave each room. Say each rent question twice, then thank the landlord with hvala before you step back into the stairwell.
tips: Keep Može? and the follow-up question in one breath.
Pair kirija with mjesečno when you talk about monthly pay.
Stay in the present even when you plan a longer stay.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B. Almost signing the lease
lessonBlocks.body: Move from the tour to the table where an ugovor waits beside a pen. Say Moraš platiti kiriju when the landlord explains house rules in plain language. Describe namještaj with ima and lijep when you point at the sofa corner. Amira asks about ključ and Ana says Želim iznajmiti stan for three months. Emir checks that kuhinja i kupatilo su čisti before he nods toward the balcony. Reuse molim and hvala with the landlord so the scene stays polite end to end. Practice a short chain aloud. Permission, rent, room names, obligation, thanks, and one calm goodbye at the door. Repeat the chain until signing feels possible even if you still need one night to decide.
tips: Reuse Imam from earlier lessons when you claim a favorite room.
Say namještaj slowly. It is a long but useful word.
End with hvala even if you need time to decide.

conversation.title: Pogled stana u Zenici
conversation.setting: Ana, Emir, and Amira visit a Zenica flat with the landlord before a possible longer stay.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.bosnian: Dobar dan. Može? Mogu pogledati stan?
lines.english: Good day. May I? Can I look at the apartment?

lines.speaker: Landlord
lines.english: Yes. Come in. This is the kitchen.

lines.speaker: Emir
lines.english: How much is the rent monthly?

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.bosnian: Soba je sunčana. Imam dobar osjećaj.
lines.english: The room is sunny. I have a good feeling.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.bosnian: Želim iznajmiti stan na tri mjeseca.
lines.english: I want to rent the apartment for three months.

lines.speaker: Landlord
lines.bosnian: Moraš platiti kiriju prvog u mjesecu.
lines.english: You must pay the rent on the first of the month.

lines.speaker: Emir
lines.english: Do we have a contract and key today?

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.english: Thank you. We will think until evening.

funFacts.title: Zenica mixes industry and student life
funFacts.body: Zenica sits in central Bosnia and Herzegovina with factories, university students, and tram lines that shape daily housing hunts. Flats near campus and the steelworks turn over quickly. Learners who visit a block staircase practice real city vocabulary rather than only café small talk.

funFacts.title: Kirija is often monthly
funFacts.body: Rent talk in Bosnia and Herzegovina usually centers on a monthly kirija figure. Landlords may write the number on a note or say it in the hallway. Learning Koliko je kirija? prepares you for that first practical question.

funFacts.title: Može is a door opener
funFacts.body: Može? at a doorway is faster than a long grammar explanation. The answer Može. invites you inside with one calm word. Present permission chunks keep housing visits friendly.

funFacts.title: Namještaj can be light
funFacts.body: Some flats come with basic namještaj while others are empty. A sofa corner and kitchen table are enough to describe a place today. Point and name rather than memorizing a furniture catalog.

civicContext.title: Returnees in Republika Srpska still face hostile local pressure
civicContext.body: Minority return to Republika Srpska remains unfinished three decades after the war. Bosniak returnees often meet segregated schooling, job barriers, and political rhetoric that treats them as outsiders in their own towns. International monitors keep documenting property disputes and intimidation around returnee communities. Legal rights to reclaim a house therefore collide with daily pressure that shrinks who can safely stay.
